10.1002_aenm.202504126: Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) with ultrahigh power density are critical components in electronic products. However, with the accelerating miniaturization and integration of electronic devices, MLCCs are confronted with the challenge of achieving high capacitive energy storage performance and excellent stability simultaneously. Herein, guided by a phase‐field simulation method, a strategic high entropy‐driven design is employed to induce atomic‐scale lattice distortions and construct nano‐scale local heterogeneous polarization configurations. This approach effectively enhances the resistivity of ceramic dielectrics, weakens the anisotropic field, and lowers the domain‐switching barrier. Benefiting from these entropy‐driven characteristics and device‐scale design, an impressively high recoverable energy storage density of 17.2 J cm −3 and an energy storage efficiency of 95.5% are achieved in the BaTiO 3 ‐based high entropy MLCCs. Notably, these MLCCs also exhibit excellent temperature stability (energy storage performance change rate <4%) within a broad temperature range of 25–150 °C, while showing an extremely low performance degradation rate (<1%) during 10 6 cycles. Moreover, this study systematically unravels the underlying mechanism linking entropy‐driven local lattice distortions, polarization configurations, and capacitive energy storage performance, thereby offering an innovative design paradigm for optimizing MLCCs energy storage via high entropy design.
10.1002_aenm.71572: Complex degradation trajectories compromise the lifetime reliability and operational safety of lithium‐ion batteries in advanced energy‐storage systems. Aging pathways induced by temperature, rate, and voltage‐abuse stresses are often entangled in conventional health‐estimation models, limiting transferable degradation representation and future‐trajectory updating under distribution shifts. Here, a generalizable, mechanism‐anchored health‐management framework is developed for lithium‐ion batteries under heterogeneous aging conditions. Using aging‐condition identification as a proxy task, we identify a degradation‐sensitive 3.3–3.4 V charging window in LiFePO 4 /graphite cells, where statistically selected features are linked to incremental‐capacity fingerprints. These electrochemically anchored features are integrated with a condition‐aware soft mixture‐of‐experts model to disentangle heterogeneous feature–state‐of‐health (SOH) relationships with and without condition labels during inference. Cross‐dataset continual learning enables adaptation to an unseen data source while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Finally, data‐driven SOH observations are assimilated into a physics‐inspired parametric degradation model through an adaptive unscented Kalman filter, converting pointwise health estimates into online‐updatable degradation trajectories. The framework achieves robust SOH estimation across multi‐stress aging conditions and stable 100–300‐step look‐ahead trajectory prediction, establishing an interpretable route from electrochemical fingerprints to trajectory‐level battery prognostics.
10.1002_anie.202524377: The ammonia electrooxidation reaction (AOR) represents a pivotal process for sustainable energy technologies, yet its mechanism on non‐precious metal catalysts remains ambiguous, primarily due to the elusive nature of key reaction intermediates. Specifically, the role of oxygen vacancies (Ov) in steering the AOR pathway is not well understood. Herein, we directly captured the hydrazine (N 2 H 4 ) intermediate, which unequivocally confirms the operation of the Gerischer–Marcus (G–M) pathway on oxygen‐deficient copper oxide (CuO). This breakthrough was enabled by an aggregation‐induced emission electrochemiluminescence (AIE‐ECL) probe, which allows quantitative, real‐time detection of N 2 H 4 with ultrahigh sensitivity (0.163 nM). The direct visualization of probe consumption via fluorescence microscopy imaging provided orthogonal validation. Combined with in situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations, we establish that oxygen vacancies (Ov) act as a “steering wheel” to preferentially stabilize N 2 H 4 and channel the reaction preferentially along the G–M route. A direct correlation between Ov concentration and N 2 H 4 accumulation is demonstrated, linking atomic‐scale defect structure to macroscopic catalytic performance. This work not only presents a paradigm for probing elusive electrocatalytic intermediates but also delivers a fundamental principle for influencing reaction pathways through defect engineering.
10.1002_cssc.71076: The conversion of osmotic energy from salinity gradients into electricity offers a sustainable and low‐intermittency source of clean power, capable of complementing existing energy systems. Membrane properties are central to the efficiency of such energy conversion; however, conventional ion‐exchange membranes often suffer from high internal resistance and limited performance. In this work, we report a Janus membrane engineered from a microporous sulfonated poly(ether sulfone) base coated with a thin, nano‐porous, positively charged crosslinked poly(vinyl alcohol)–poly(ethyleneimine) layer. The asymmetric architecture promotes directional ion transport, selectivity, and reduced resistance, leading to high osmotic energy harvesting. The membrane achieved a maximum power density of 0.38 W m −2 and a current density of 18 A m −2 under a 50‐fold KCl concentration gradient at ambient temperature. The power density further increased to 0.705 W m −2 upon introducing a 30 °C temperature differential, attributed to enhanced ion mobility and improved surface‐charge regulation. In flow capacitive deionization applications, the Janus membrane exhibited an excellent salt adsorption capacity of 4.21 mg g −1 at 1.2 V in 1 g L −1 NaCl solution, demonstrating efficient desalination performance. These results highlight the potential of the developed asymmetric Janus membrane as a cost‐effective and robust platform for simultaneous osmotic energy harvesting and water desalination.
10.1002_smll.76154: Aqueous Zn–S batteries offer high theoretical energy density and intrinsic safety, but iodine‐mediated sulfur conversion introduces severe chemical and electrochemical instability at Zn anode. Herein, life‐cycle‐resolved three‐electrode measurements reveal that, although sulfur utilization gradually decreases, the rapid growth of Zn anode polarization and eventual internal short circuit dominate terminal cell failure. Guided by this failure diagnosis, iodoacetamide (IAM) is introduced as a multifunctional additive to couple interphase and solvation regulation. Interfacial spectroscopy and depth profiling indicate the in situ formation of a gradient interphase comprising an N‐containing organic‐rich outer region and a ZnS/ZnSO 3 ‐rich inorganic inner region, which suppresses polyiodide corrosion and homogenizes Zn 2+ flux. Spectroscopic analyses and molecular simulations further show that IAM modulates the local Zn 2+ coordination environment and water hydrogen‐bond network, accompanied by enhanced ion pairing and a lower apparent interfacial activation barrier for Zn deposition. As a result, Zn||Cu cells achieve over 2000 cycles with an average coulombic efficiency of 99.91%, while full Zn–S cells retain 484.5 mAh g −1 after 550 cycles at 20 A g −1 , corresponding to 75.95% capacity retention (27.26% without IAM). This work highlights the need to balance iodine‐enabled sulfur conversion with Zn stability, offering a practical design principle for durable aqueous Zn–S batteries.
10.1038_s41467-026-75847-3: Solar-driven interfacial evaporation (SDIE) is a sustainable, carbon-neutral approach for freshwater production. Nevertheless, achieving both high evaporation rates and efficient removal remains challenging, especially for wastewater enriched with concentrated ions and strongly polar VOCs from chemical and electronics manufacturing. Here, we report the confined water-selective highways within a densified photothermal membrane (DPM) for ultrafast purification of such complex wastewater. Through mechanical compression and the rational selection of hydrophilic polymers, DPM’s interlayer nanostructures and chemical environments are engineered with molecular precision. Due to the synergistic effect of steric hindrance and chemical selectivity, this structure enables preferential water transport while effectively excluding highly concentrated ions and strongly polar VOCs. DPM exhibits a high water evaporation rate of 2.58 kg m − 2 h − 1 under 1 kW m − 2 . DPM retains stable performance for over 200 h in various near-saturated hypersaline solutions (20 wt% salinity) and enables clean water harvesting from both common (e.g., benzene, toluene, phenol) and strongly polar VOCs (e.g., ethanol, isopropanol, n-butanol) even at very high concentrations. Device integration further demonstrates its scalability for treating complex wastewater, highlighting the significance of molecularly engineered interfacial architectures for efficient SDIE under challenging conditions.
